Lewis acid-catalyzed divergent synthesis of polysubstituted furans and pyrroles†
Check for updates
Cite this: Org Chem Front , 2025, 12, 2173
Chenguang Li,<sup>a</sup> Tongxiang Cao \*<sup>a</sup> and Shifa Zhu \*<sup>a,b</sup>
Received 24th November 2024, Accepted 27th January 2025
rsc.li/frontiers-organic

The development of an advisable strategy to obtain biologically relevant polysubstituted furans and pyrroles is a highly anticipated yet challenging task. Here we report an eficient synthetic strategy for the rapid construction of multisubstituted C2-furan or pyrrole carboxylic acid derivatives via a cascade reaction from simple and readily available starting materials. This catalytic protocol, characterized by inexpensive Lewis catalysts and high atom economy, provides access to a wide variety of tri-, and tetrasubstituted furan/pyrrole derivatives in excellent yields. Gram-scale synthesis and synthetic applications are demonstrated

Five-membered heterocycles are very important fundamental heterocyclic motifs widely found in diverse applications of organic materials, pharmaceutical science and synthetic chemistry.<sup>1</sup> Among these heterocyclic molecules, densely functionalized furans and pyrroles have garnered a particular interest since they are the primary constituents of many natural products that have special biological activities, pharmaceuticals, and organic materials such as photographic chemicals and optoelectronic materials.<sup>2</sup> In particular, furan derivatives with long-chain carboxylic acids, like furan fatty acids (FuFAs), constitute an important class of biologically relevant natural products due to their anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular activities, afording significant nutritional health benefits to humans (Scheme 1a).<sup>3</sup> N-Aryl pyrrole derivatives have also exhibited intriguing bioactivities ranging from antibacterial, antiviral, anti-inflammatory, and antitumoral properties (Scheme 1a).<sup>4</sup> It is consequently not surprising that the development of diverse methods to synthesize functionalized furans and pyrroles is an area of intense research in modern organic chemistry.

The widely reported synthetic methods of these heterocyclic compounds are of great concern and can be broadly classified into two categories.<sup>5</sup> One is the functionalization of an existing furan or pyrrole ring.<sup>6</sup> Another involves the heteroatommediated cyclization of an acyclic substrate to construct a heterocyclic ring, with all or most of the desired substituents pre-installed on the precursor, via classical methods (Paal– Knorr,<sup>7</sup> Hantzsch,<sup>8</sup> and Feist–Benary<sup>9</sup> reactions) or the present catalytic methods.<sup>10</sup> Thus far, only a few methods to access C2- substituted furanyl carboxylic acid derivatives have been reported through the two strategies mentioned.<sup>11</sup> For example, Kimber and co-workers realized the first total synthesis of the tetrasubstituted furan fatty acid (FFA) metabolite 5-[(1E)-2-car-

Volla’s group reported a convergent strategy for preparing γ-furan-3-yl carboxylic acid derivatives via a Pd(II)-catalyzed intramolecular cascade cyclization of alkyne-diols followed by hydrocarbofunctionalization of unactivated alkenes employing a cleavable 8-aminoquinoline directing group (Scheme 1b).<sup>11a</sup> A complementary protocol for accessing γ-furan-2-yl carboxylic acid derivatives was also developed by carrying out the reaction in a tandem manner.

Although the present methods are eficiently applied to obtain diferently substituted furans and pyrroles, these methodologies generally require the use of expensive or air-sensitive transition-metal catalysts and have poor accessibility of the starting materials with limited substrate scopes.<sup>12</sup> Therefore, the development of new strategies that facilitate the rapid construction of furans or pyrroles with multiple functional groups is still a challenging topic, and new protocols for addressing the issue are still highly desirable. As a continuation of our interest in the synthesis of functionalized (benzo)furans through transition metal catalysis,<sup>13</sup> we hereby describe a divergent method involving two inexpensive Lewis acids for the construction of diverse C2-functionalized furanyl/pyrrolyl carboxylic acid derivatives in good yields (Scheme 1c).

We commenced our investigation by exploring the model reaction between β-ketoallene 1a and aniline 2a, using 10 mol% Ph PAuCl as the catalyst and NaBARF (12 mol%) as a halide scavenger in toluene at room temperature under ${ \bf N } _ { 2 }$ for 5 h, which aforded the desired furan product 3aa in 25% yield and the unexpected pyrrole product 4aa, albeit in 5% yield (Table 1, entry 1). Significant improvement was not observed with higher temperature, possibly due to the decomposition of substrate 1a or failure to condense with aniline 2a (see Table S1† for more details). To our delight, inexpensive Zn (OTf ) and Bi(OTf ) showed good selectivity and eficiency to respectively provide 3aa in 92% yield and 4aa in 66% yield when we turned to screening diferent Lewis acid catalysts, although most of them have shown disappointing results (Table 1, entries 2–10). Moreover, decreasing the aniline 2a load to 1.5 equiv. was also found to be efective in providing 3aa in 92% yield, while lowering the temperature to 80 °C resulted in a decrease in the yield of 3aa to 62% (Table 1, entries 11 and 12), and a further decrease in the employed amount of aniline 2a to 1.2 or 1.0 equiv. caused a slight decrease in the amount of 3aa (see Table S2 of the ESI†). text: S3†), we were delighted to observe that cyclohexane rendered the best result for the transformation with 1a and 2a employing 10 mol% Bi(OTf) to deliver 4aa in 83% yield (Table 1, entry 13). Interestingly, as the reaction proceeded, we observed that some products were precipitated from the reaction system, revealing one possible reason why cyclohexane is superior to other solvents. The structure of 3aa was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray difraction (see the ESI† for details).

Further experiments were then conducted to explore the generality of the cascade reaction concerning a variety of aromatic amines with cyclic β-ketoallenes. As shown in Scheme 2, a variety of multisubstituted furans were competently synthesized. The protocol first succeeded with a variety of primary anilines bearing para substituents, whereas the electronic perturbation of substituents had a distinct influence on the reaction eficiency. Aniline, 4-methyl aniline, and 4-tert-butyl aniline engaged in reactivity using β-ketoallene 2a, with the desired furans 3aa–3ac formed in 78–92% isolated yields. For the para-methoxy variant, the desired product 3ad was furnished in 58% yield. The conversion of 4-halogeno anilines with compound 2a also proceeded smoothly, delivering products 3af–3ah in good isolated yields (70–95%). Gratifyingly, the anilines having diferent electron-withdrawing groups at the para position, such as trifluoromethoxy, nitro and trifluoromethyl, were also eficiently converted into the corresponding products 3ae–3aj in 87%, 82% and 85% yields, respectively, while 4-cyano aniline slowly transformed into 3ak in 56% yield with 30 h of heating. Meanwhile, the ortho-methyl and -phenyl substituted anilines could also be tolerated, generating the corresponding products 3ap and 3au in slightly lower yields of 58% and 74%. However, other substituents at either the ortho or meta position could also aford the corresponding products 3al–3aq in excellent yields (84–93%). In addition, di- and multi-substituted anilines 2r and 2s can also obtain the target products with distinct yields (83% and 37%) due to the significant steric hindrance. 1-Naphthylamine 2t bearing a strong conjugated aromatic system and 3,4-(methylenedioxy)aniline 2v could also ofer the target products in good yields (3at and 3av, 75–81%). Particularly, changing primary aromatic amines to secondary aromatic amines was compatible with the synthesis of the desired products 3aw–3ay in moderate to good yields (46–91%).

text: Subsequently, we turned our attention to defining the capacity of diferent cyclic β-allenyl 1,3-diketones in this reaction to react with aniline. With respect to the substituents at the $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ position, both electron-rich and electron-deficient substituents on the phenyl group (1b–1h) could be employed for this transformation, and the corresponding tetrasubstituted furans 3ba–3ga were achieved in modest to good yields (46–87%). The nature of the substituents had a demonstrable efect on this reaction. As for the electron-withdrawing 4-nitro and 4-Br groups, 3ga and 3fa were aforded in modest yields. Moreover, product 3ha containing the sterically hindered 2-methylphenyl substituent was provided in 83% yield. It is noted that when monosubstituted allene 1i was tested, the reaction provided the corresponding furan product 3ia in 50% yield. When $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ was methyl in the allene substrate, 3ja could still be obtained in 82% yield.

Next, a series of oxygen nucleophiles was then explored under identical conditions to synthesize various tetrasubstituted furan derivatives (Scheme 3). C2-substituted furan carboxylic acid 5aa was obtained quantitatively in the presence of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ At the same time, three diferent ester derivatives 5ab– 5ad could be separated in high yields (89–95%) with phenol, benzyl alcohol and N-hydroxyphthalimide as nucleophiles.

Similarly, with the corresponding optimal reaction conditions in hand, we next explored the substrate scope for the synthesis of pyrroles (Scheme 4). Overall, various substituted aromatic amine compounds with electron-donating and -withdrawing groups could undergo reactions smoothly with moderate to good yields (67–88%). To our delight, benzylamine 2h could also be tolerated with generating product 4ah in 33% isolated yield. The efect of diferent substituents on the allene substrates was investigated. It was found that various substituents on the phenyl group of $\scriptstyle \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ had an impact on the reactions. Electron-donating groups resulted in relatively lower yields than electron-withdrawing ones (4ba–4ga, 38–76%). It is noted that when the methyl group was placed at the ortho position of the phenyl group, the reaction gave the desired product 4ia in 33% yield. When monosubstituted allene 1i and 1,3-disubstituted allene 1k were utilized as the substrates, the reaction gave products 4ia and 4ka in 81% and 86% yields, respectively. When $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ was a methyl group and $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { R } } ^ { 3 }$ was H, the reaction still proceeded smoothly to aford the desired product in good yield (4ja, 66%). β-Ketoallene 1l with a 1,3-cyclopentanedione ring was investigated as well, successfully providing the desired product 4la in 86% yield.

To further explore the eficiency, practicality, and generality of the reaction protocol presented here, relevant studies were conducted (Scheme 5b). First, the furan products 3aa and 5ad could also be obtained in comparable yields (79% and 70%) on a gram scale (3.5 mmol). Downstream transformations of the furan moiety were then carried out. Through a [4 + 2] cycloaddition,<sup>13g</sup> treatments of 3aa with dienophiles, such as DMAD and benzyne, produced Diels–Alder adducts 8 and 9 in good yields. Decarboxylative conjugate addition and hydrodecarboxylation of aliphatic N-(acyloxy)phthalimide 5ad were also performed through photoirradiation with Hantzsch ester in N,N-dimethylacetamide solution,<sup>14</sup> furnishing the corresponding products 10 and 11 in 89 and 37% yields, respectively.

A plausible reaction mechanism for this cascade protocol has been proposed in Scheme 6. Initially, β-ketoallene 1 is activated by Lewis acid catalysts to form a dual-coordinated adduct I with the allene moiety and the oxygen of the carbonyl group, which display distinct activity depending on the catalytic metals. The catalytic zinc center might slightly favour coordination to the allene moiety over the oxygen, thus triggering an intramolecular 5-exo-trig cyclization to form an oxonium intermediate II-a. In the absence of nucleophiles, the reaction is almost shut down with a large amount of β-ketoallene 1 being preserved, and no Friedel–Crafts cyclization product 12 is observed. Therefore, we postulated that the resulting II-a is sluggish to undergo fragmentation to form the acyl cation II-b. If a very small amount of transient II-b is formed, it would be trapped by excessive external nucleophiles in an irreversible manner, thus driving the processes toward the desired product. In contrast, the bismuth catalyst might have a stronger afinity to oxygen than the allene moiety, resulting in a more active carbonyl group, which is subsequently captured by aniline to give geminal amino alcohol III and then undergoes bismuth-assisted dehydration to form ketimine IV.<sup>12a,15</sup> Finally, the more nucleophilic ketimine engages the activated allene moiety through a similar 5-exo-trig cyclization, followed by a fragmentation–trapping process to furnish pyrrole 4.
Conclusions

In summary, we have developed an operationally simple, unified strategy for the synthesis of diversely substituted C2-furan or pyrrole carboxylic acid derivatives via a cascade reaction from simple and readily available/preparable starting materials. The cascade is proposed to go through consecutive processes of cyclization, ring fragmentation, aromatization and an $\mathrm { S } _ { \mathrm { N } } 1$ reaction involving acyl cation species as the key intermediate. This catalytic protocol, characterized by inexpensive catalysts and high atom economy, provides access to a wide variety of tri- and tetrasubstituted furan/pyrrole derivatives in excellent yields. In addition, the cyclization– fragmentation strategy was studied for its generality and scalability by carrying out gram-scale synthesis and downstream synthetic transformations. This methodology might also provide a potential synthetic route to tetrasubstituted furan fatty acids.
